title: Does a small neural roll controller beat the three-gain PID on a randomised quadrotor, and does it change which airframe is best?
lede: does a 31-parameter neural roll controller beat the three-gain PID on a randomised quadrotor? Not at equal evaluations (7.7° PID against 9.0°); with 10× the evaluations it only matches it (7.6°), and the airframe ranking is unchanged (Spearman 1.00).
summary: Follow-up to codesign-aero-robust: a 6-unit tanh network (31 parameters) trained by CMA-ES replaces the three-gain PID roll law on six airframes spanning the wide-plant ranking, three seeds each, scored on 64 held-out wide-plant episodes. At the same 96 evaluations the network is worse on 5 of 6 airframes (mean 8.96° against 7.72°); at 960 evaluations it matches the PID (7.59°, gains of 0.00 to 0.09° on five airframes and 0.53° on one). The best airframe and the ranking (Spearman 1.00) do not change, so the three-gain law did not distort the earlier sizing result. Limits: evolution strategies rather than PPO, no skip path, six airframes, roll only; the plant and randomisation ranges are assumed round numbers carried over from codesign-aero, not measurements.
